title: Acute Limb Ischemia: Sudden Pain and Perfusion Loss Is a Vascular Emergency
bottomLine: Sudden severe limb pain, pallor, coolness, sensory or motor change, and diminished perfusion can indicate acute limb ischemia. Escalate immediately because tissue viability is time-sensitive.
recognize: New pain at rest, cool/pale limb, delayed capillary refill, sensory loss, weakness/paralysis, and pulse change are concerning; pulse loss is late and should not be awaited.
priorities: Compare bilateral neurovascular findings, protect the limb, and activate urgent vascular evaluation.
assessMonitor: Trend pain, color, temperature, capillary refill, sensation, movement, Doppler/pulses if trained, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Avoid heat, compression, massage, or delays; maintain ordered NPO/IV support while preparing for definitive care.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation, thrombolysis, and revascularization strategy are provider-led and bleeding-risk dependent.
teaching: Sudden limb pain or numbness with color/temperature change needs emergency evaluation.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; acute neurovascular deterioration requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for a completely absent pulse before escalating severe ischemic symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Threatened limb tissue is a clock—escalate before paralysis or pulse loss.

title: Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia: Rest Pain, Wounds, or Gangrene Need Rapid Vascular Follow-Up
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Ischemic rest pain, nonhealing wounds, or gangrene suggest chronic limb-threatening ischemia. Protect tissue, assess infection/perfusion, and escalate for vascular evaluation rather than treating the wound alone.
recognize: Pain at rest, dependent rubor, cool foot, poor healing, tissue loss, and gangrene are high-risk cues.
priorities: Assess perfusion and wound status together and report progressive ischemia or infection.
assessMonitor: Trend skin color/temp, pain, wound size/drainage, sensation, pulses/Doppler if trained, glucose control, and infection cues.
interventions: Offload/protect the limb and coordinate wound/vascular care; avoid constrictive dressings unless specifically ordered.
medicationSafety: Antiplatelet, lipid-lowering, antihypertensive, and diabetes therapy require medication reconciliation and adherence support.
teaching: Report new ulcers, black tissue, or rest pain promptly and avoid tobacco exposure.
delegationScope: Skin checks may be delegated; ischemia interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Focusing only on topical wound care while missing progressive arterial insufficiency.
oneLinePearl: A nonhealing ischemic wound is a perfusion problem first.

title: Suspected DVT: Unilateral Swelling and Pain Need Evaluation, Not Massage
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: New unilateral limb swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, or discoloration can indicate DVT. Limit unnecessary manipulation, escalate for diagnostic evaluation, and assess for pulmonary embolism symptoms.
recognize: Recent surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum, estrogen exposure, prior VTE, and central lines increase risk.
priorities: Assess cardiopulmonary symptoms and notify the clinical team promptly.
assessMonitor: Compare limb appearance/circumference as appropriate, pain, warmth, vital signs, oxygenation, and chest symptoms.
interventions: Avoid massage or vigorous limb manipulation and follow the ordered mobility/anticoagulation plan.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant initiation, hold parameters, and dose depend on diagnosis, renal function, bleeding risk, and orders.
teaching: Report sudden breathing difficulty or chest pain immediately.
delegationScope: Measurements may be delegated; VTE recognition/escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Massaging a painful swollen calf to improve circulation.
oneLinePearl: Suspected DVT: assess, protect, escalate—do not massage.

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Sudden Dyspnea, Pleuritic Pain, or Syncope Is an Emergency
bottomLine: Unexplained sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, hemoptysis, or syncope can indicate pulmonary embolism. Activate emergency evaluation and support oxygenation and hemodynamics.
recognize: Symptoms may be subtle; recent DVT risk factors increase concern.
priorities: Assess ABCs, oxygenation, hemodynamics, and summon emergency help.
assessMonitor: Continuous respiratory status, SpO2, BP/HR, mental status, chest pain, and ordered cardiopulmonary findings.
interventions: Position for breathing, provide oxygen if indicated/ordered, maintain IV access, and prepare for diagnostic and anticoagulation/reperfusion management.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation and thrombolysis are high-risk, diagnosis- and bleeding-risk-dependent therapies.
teaching: After stabilization, reinforce anticoagulant safety and recurrence warning signs.
delegationScope: Emergency support is immediate; diagnostic and reperfusion decisions are provider-led.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because the lungs sound clear despite sudden hypoxemia and pleuritic pain.
oneLinePearl: PE can have clear lungs—sudden dyspnea plus risk factors still demands escalation.

title: Possible AAA Rupture: Back or Abdominal Pain With Shock Requires Immediate Action
bottomLine: Sudden severe abdominal, back, or flank pain with hypotension, syncope, pallor, or a known aneurysm can indicate abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture. Treat as internal hemorrhage and mobilize emergency vascular care.
recognize: Shock may occur with little or no external blood loss.
priorities: ABCs, emergency activation, rapid IV/blood-readiness support, and NPO status as ordered.
assessMonitor: BP/HR, mental status, skin perfusion, pain, abdominal findings, urine output, and signs of ongoing shock.
interventions: Minimize delays and unnecessary abdominal manipulation; prepare for emergent surgery or endovascular care.
medicationSafety: Hemodynamic targets and blood products are protocol/provider directed; avoid casually treating pain while delaying definitive evaluation.
teaching: Known aneurysm patients should seek emergency care for sudden severe abdominal/back pain or fainting.
delegationScope: Emergency observations/support may be shared; definitive management is provider-led.
examTrap: Waiting for a pulsatile mass before treating shock as possible aneurysm rupture.
oneLinePearl: AAA rupture can bleed entirely inside the body—shock is the clue.

title: After Limb Revascularization: New Pain or Neurovascular Change Requires Immediate Reassessment
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After vascular intervention, recurrent severe pain, pallor or coolness, pulse/Doppler change, swelling, bleeding, or neurologic loss can signal re-occlusion, bleeding, compartment syndrome, or reperfusion injury.
recognize: Compare with the documented postprocedure baseline rather than relying on one isolated pulse check.
priorities: Perform focused neurovascular and access-site assessment and escalate acute change.
assessMonitor: Pain, color/temp, capillary refill, sensation, movement, pulses/Doppler if trained, access-site bleeding/hematoma, urine output, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Protect the limb and access site; follow ordered bedrest, positioning, and vascular monitoring protocol.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic therapy increases bleeding risk but should not be stopped independently without urgent clinical review.
teaching: Report recurrent severe pain, numbness, coldness, or bleeding immediately.
delegationScope: Routine vitals may be delegated; neurovascular deterioration requires licensed interpretation.
examTrap: Calling severe postprocedure pain expected without reassessing perfusion.
oneLinePearl: After revascularization, compare every limb finding with the new baseline.

title: Venous Ulcer Care: Compression Requires Arterial Safety Screening
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Venous ulcers often benefit from compression, but significant arterial disease changes compression safety. Confirm the ordered vascular assessment and plan before applying high-pressure compression.
recognize: Edema, gaiter-region skin changes, and shallow irregular ulcers suggest venous disease; cool foot, ischemic rest pain, or poor pulses suggest arterial compromise.
priorities: Assess wound plus perfusion and verify the compression order/vascular plan.
assessMonitor: Edema, wound size/drainage, skin changes, pain, foot temperature/color, pulses/Doppler if trained, and tolerance of compression.
interventions: Elevate and use prescribed compression when appropriate; protect skin and promote mobility as ordered.
medicationSafety: Diuretics do not substitute for venous compression and mobility when those are clinically indicated.
teaching: Report new numbness, severe pain, or coldness after compression.
delegationScope: Compression application depends on competency/policy and an established plan.
examTrap: Applying strong compression to a cool painful foot without arterial assessment.
oneLinePearl: Compression treats venous pressure only when arterial inflow is safe enough.
sourceBasis: Contemporary U.S. vascular and wound-care principles

title: After Carotid Intervention: Neck Swelling or New Neuro Deficit Is an Emergency
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After carotid surgery or stenting, new weakness, speech/vision change, severe headache, neck swelling, airway symptoms, or bleeding can indicate stroke, hyperperfusion, hematoma, or hemorrhage.
recognize: Neck hematoma can threaten the airway rapidly.
priorities: Assess airway and neurologic status and activate surgical/stroke response for acute change.
assessMonitor: Neuro checks, BP per protocol, neck site, swallowing/voice, respiratory status, and bleeding.
interventions: Maintain emergency airway readiness and ordered positioning/activity restrictions.
medicationSafety: Antiplatelet/anticoagulant management is procedure-specific and prescriber directed.
teaching: Report new neurologic symptoms, neck swelling, or breathing difficulty immediately.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; acute neuro/airway change requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Focusing on the incision while missing subtle new aphasia.
oneLinePearl: After carotid procedures, protect both brain and airway.

title: Arterial Access Hematoma: Bleeding Can Expand Quickly
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After arterial catheterization, new swelling, firmness, persistent bleeding, severe pain, hypotension, or distal perfusion change can indicate significant access-site bleeding or vascular injury.
recognize: Femoral bleeding may track internally; radial complications can threaten hand perfusion.
priorities: Assess hemodynamics, access site, and distal neurovascular status and escalate promptly.
assessMonitor: Site size/firmness, bleeding, BP/HR, pain, limb color/temp, sensation/movement, and pulses/Doppler if trained.
interventions: Apply ordered/manual pressure per protocol if active external bleeding and maintain prescribed limb restrictions.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic therapy may worsen bleeding but must not be stopped independently without urgent review.
teaching: Report swelling, bleeding, severe pain, numbness, or coldness immediately.
delegationScope: Site observation may be delegated; bleeding/perfusion interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Marking the hematoma border and simply rechecking later despite hypotension.
oneLinePearl: Access-site swelling plus instability is active bleeding until proven otherwise.

title: Chronic Venous Insufficiency: Sudden Asymmetry Is Not Routine Edema
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Chronic venous edema may be longstanding, but new unilateral worsening, pain, warmth, or erythema requires evaluation for DVT, cellulitis, or another acute process rather than being labeled baseline venous disease.
recognize: Baseline edema may fluctuate with dependency; abrupt asymmetry or pain is a change in condition.
priorities: Compare with baseline and assess for VTE/infection cues.
assessMonitor: Edema distribution, skin temperature/color, pain, wounds, mobility, cardiopulmonary symptoms, and weight trends.
interventions: Use prescribed elevation/compression/mobility plan and escalate acute changes.
medicationSafety: Do not reflexively increase diuretics for localized venous edema without clinical review.
teaching: Know the usual edema pattern and report abrupt one-sided changes.
delegationScope: Routine skin/edema observation may be delegated; acute-change interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Calling new unilateral swelling chronic venous insufficiency without checking for DVT.
oneLinePearl: Baseline venous edema can be chronic; sudden asymmetry is acute until assessed.
